title: Boundary states, slices, and a free shortcut
intro: Accumulation read off two endpoints — and the symmetry check that can settle it before you start.

steps.title: Two evaluations settle it
steps.body:
The Second FTC says `∫ₐᵇ f dx = F(b) - F(a)`: an accumulation read from its boundary states, with nothing in the interior examined. `∫₀⁴(-x² + 4x) dx` has antiderivative `-x³/3 + 2x²`, giving `(-64/3 + 32) - 0 = 32/3 ≈ 10.667`.

That is why a rocket's **total impulse** `I = ∫F dt = m·Δv` comes from the burn's endpoints, and why a capacitor's `V(t) = (1/C)∫₀ᵗ I dτ + V(0)` carries its initial condition explicitly — the + C from the previous concept, sitting in the formula where it belongs.

steps.title: What software actually does
steps.body:
Closed-form antiderivatives are a luxury most real integrands don't offer, so solvers slice. The trapezoidal rule on `∫₀⁴(-x² + 4x)`:

| Slices N | Error |
|---|---|
| 10 | 0.1067 |
| 20 | 0.0267 |
| 40 | 0.0067 |

The error **quarters as N doubles** — the 1/N² signature, and the honest reason you double resolution rather than nudge it. A PID controller's integral term is this same running sum, accumulating error every clock tick.

steps.title: Check parity before integrating anything
steps.body:
On symmetric bounds [-a, a], the integrand's symmetry can settle the answer before any work starts. **Odd** (f(-x) = -f(x)) integrates to exactly **0**. **Even** (f(-x) = f(x)) gives `2∫₀ᵃ`, halving the work.

This is an O(1) guard in front of an O(N) computation — the same instinct as rejecting a collision pair by bounding box before the real test. Across a symmetric delta wing, **lift is even** and accumulates while **roll moment is odd** and cancels; in AC, net voltage over a cycle is odd and vanishes while power is even and piles up, which is why a device with zero average voltage still gets hot.

viz.title: Three routes to the same number

points.label: Second FTC
points.note: F(b) − F(a). Exact and instant — when an antiderivative exists in closed form, which is the part real problems rarely grant.

points.label: Trapezoid
points.note: Slices; error ~1/N². What numerical libraries do. Converges to the exact value as N grows.

points.label: Parity
points.note: Odd ⇒ 0 with no computation at all. Even ⇒ half the work. Free, and only available if you look before you integrate.

steps.title: Area between two curves
steps.body:
`A = ∫ₐᵇ [upper - lower] dx`, with a and b solved from where the curves cross. Both halves are where mistakes live: picking the wrong curve as upper flips the sign, and guessing the bounds instead of solving for intersections computes a region nobody asked about.

The standard check: `y = x + 2` against `y = x²` meet at x = -1 and x = 2 and enclose exactly **9/2**. Verify an area routine against closed forms you know — πr² for a circle, πab for an ellipse — because one that gets those wrong will get your airfoil section wrong too, just less visibly.

recap: The FTC turns accumulation into two evaluations. When no antiderivative exists, slices converge as 1/N². On symmetric bounds, check parity first — odd is zero for free. And for area between curves, solve for the intersections rather than guessing the bounds.
